newsitem.title: USA: Republicans ask whether Dole ran right campaign.
newsitem.headline: Republicans ask whether Dole ran right campaign.

text.p: With the Republicans retaining both the Senate and the House, a great debate is about to begin -- could Bob Dole have won the White House if he ran a different campaign or even just a better one?
Or with the country still tipping in a conservative direction, could the Republicans have won with a different candidate?

Many Republicans have wondered -- both privately and publicly -- whether Dole undermined his own cause by running a campaign short on rhetoric, issues, manpower, money, campaign stops, input from others, energy sometimes and luck at other times.

In his gracious concession speech on Tuesday night, Dole said he had done his best and added, "I have never been prouder in my life than to have been the Republican nominee for the president of the United States."

In an age when television provides the audience more than crowds at campaign stops, Dole flew around the country refusing to do local television interviews. He refused to learn the medium, he refused to speak in the sound-bites it requires and when he did, the punch lines were often lost in a mumble.

Until he decided on a 96-hour marathon to end his campaign, Dole was stingy in his campaign stops, often doing just one or two a day, usually in Republican strongholds. He also travelled for a long time with only one senior aide aboard his plane rather than an entourage.
His aides had to fight with the stubborn 73-year-old Kansan to use a teleprompter to give a speech. Many times they lost and he would ramble on in a repetitive stream of consciousness.

The press corps on his plane had a contest called the "Trifecta" -- trying to guess which phrase he would use that day that was repeated three times -- whether it was "liberal, liberal, liberal" or "America, America, America."
New York Senator Alfonse D'Amato reportedly told a private Harvard University meeting that Dole had grown bored with the campaign, an idea that struck many as possibly true.

But whether Dole had or not, he had a Herculean task -- to beat an incumbent president at a time of economic prosperity and domestic tranquility. Things were good, Americans seemed to be saying. Why bother to change horses?

Dole decided to make a 15 percent tax cut the centrepiece of his campaign. Conservative columnist George Will said it was the wrong message and that he could have won if he had stressed social issues instead of economic ones.

But polls showed that the Republicans were on the wrong side, as far as a majority of Americans were concerned, on many of the social issues -- especially with women voters who overwelmingly were supporting Clinton.
Dole seldom raised the issue of whether abortions should be legal or not because it had divided his party and the country. It was a no-win situation.

Although he made a popular choice in picking Jack Kemp as his running mate, Kemp presented a problem. Vice presidential candidates have a special place in American politics -- they are the attack dogs of the campaign and Kemp refused to bite.
So the job of attacking president Clinton's fell to Dole and his attacks often just added to the reputation he had earned in 1976 as President Gerald Ford's runningmate -- the hatchet man.
But in the end, even though he lost, pollster Bob Teeter said the election proved that "Nobody loves Bill Clinton and nobody hates Bob Dole."
"We were never able to jolt the race," Dole's manager Scott Reed told the New Yorker magazine this week.
Now Republicans are wondering was Clinton just unbeatable in a year when things were going well or could another candidate -- retired Gen. Colin Powell -- have sent Clinton packing.
